content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: `workflow_dispatch` supports manual runs and typed inputs; validate inputs and use them to choose controlled behavior rather than building unsafe shell commands. Choose triggers deliberately. Event type, branch/tag filters, path filters, activity types, and token-trigger behavior determine when automation runs. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

content_blocks.code:
name: Manual preview
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      target:
        description: "Non-production target label"
        required: true
        type: choice
        options: [preview, staging]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  preview:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          TARGET: ${{ inputs.target }}
        run: echo "Selected target=$TARGET"
content_blocks.expected_output: The operator selects `preview` or `staging`, and the step reports the chosen label without deploying anything.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Open the workflow in Actions, choose Run workflow, and try each permitted value.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Remove the sample workflow after validating the input behavior.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to manual workflow execution. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain manual workflow execution, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Choose triggers and filters that run the right validation at the right time without exposing privileged jobs.

content.task: Apply manual workflow execution to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: `workflow_dispatch` supports manual runs and typed inputs; validate inputs and use them to choose controlled behavior rather than building unsafe shell commands.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: `workflow_dispatch` supports manual runs and typed inputs; validate inputs and use them to choose controlled behavior rather than building unsafe shell commands. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: `workflow_dispatch` supports manual runs and typed inputs; validate inputs and use them to choose controlled behavior rather than building unsafe shell commands.
Choose triggers deliberately. Event type, branch/tag filters, path filters, activity types, and token-trigger behavior determine when automation runs.
Use the provided example as a starting point, replace placeholders with repository-specific checks, and validate both success and expected failure behavior before publication.
